lead: You can compute double and triple integrals by slicing a region into thin pieces and adding them. You can change coordinates when circles, cylinders or spheres make Cartesian limits awkward. You can use these integrals to find area and volume.
about: This unit turns integration into two and three dimensions. Chapter 5.1 defines the double integral and evaluates it as two nested ordinary integrals using Fubini's theorem. Chapter 5.2 shows how to redraw the region and reverse the order when the given order is hard. Chapter 5.3 changes Cartesian variables to polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates, with the Jacobian factor. Chapter 5.4 extends the same nested-limit idea to triple integrals over solids. Chapter 5.5 uses these integrals to measure area and volume. After the unit you can set limits from a sketch, choose a helpful coordinate system, and compute areas and volumes without memorising separate formulas.

chapters.idea: A double integral over a rectangle can be computed as two ordinary integrals, in either order.
chapters.depth: Define the double integral as a limit of Riemann sums over a rectangle. State Fubini's theorem for continuous f on a rectangle and for simple regions, and evaluate type I and type II regions. Some syllabi call these repeated integrals or iterated integrals.

figure.aria: A flow from the double integral to the inner x-integral, the outer y-integral, and the value 4.

chapters.example: Evaluate ∬_R (x + 2y) dA over R = [0,2]×[0,1]. Both orders give 4.
chapters.trap: The inner limits must belong to the inner variable; a non-rectangular region needs variable limits in at least one direction.
chapters.leave: Change of order goes to 5.2; polar, cylindrical and spherical substitutions go to 5.3.

chapters.idea: Swapping dx dy to dy dx can turn a hard integral into an easy one after you redraw the region.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Reverse the order for type I and type II regions: sketch the region, read new bounds from the same inequalities, then integrate. Exam wording is change the order of integration.

figure.aria: A flow from the hard dy dx order to a triangle sketch, then the easy dx dy order and the value (e−1)/2.

chapters.example: Evaluate ∫_0^1 ∫_x^1 e^(y²) dy dx by changing the order; the answer is (e−1)/2.
chapters.trap: Swapping limits without redrawing the region gives wrong bounds. The new inner limits can depend on the new outer variable.
chapters.leave: Polar and other coordinate changes go to 5.3.

chapters.idea: A substitution with a Jacobian changes a double or triple integral into simpler coordinates.
chapters.depth: Polar: x = r cosθ, y = r sinθ, dA = r dr dθ. Cylindrical: x = r cosθ, y = r sinθ, z = z, dV = r dz dr dθ. Spherical: x = ρ sinφ cosθ, y = ρ sinφ sinθ, z = ρ cosφ, dV = ρ² sinφ dρ dφ dθ. Use the Jacobian from Unit 4.

figure.aria: A flow from a disk to polar substitution, the Jacobian factor r dr dθ, and the value π(1−e⁻⁴).

chapters.example: Evaluate ∬_D e^(−(x²+y²)) dA over the disk x²+y² ≤ 4; the answer is π(1−e⁻⁴).
chapters.trap: Do not forget the Jacobian: r in polar, r in cylindrical, and ρ² sinφ in spherical.
chapters.leave: Triple integrals go to 5.4; area and volume go to 5.5.

chapters.idea: A triple integral over a solid is three nested ordinary integrals with limits read from the solid.
chapters.depth: Define the triple integral over a box and extend by Fubini. Evaluate simple solids by choosing an order and reading limits from inequalities. Some syllabi call this triple integration.

figure.aria: A flow from the unit cube to inner dx, middle dy, outer dz, and the value 3/2.

chapters.example: Evaluate ∭_B (x+y+z) dV over B = [0,1]×[0,1]×[0,1]; the answer is 3/2.
chapters.trap: For a non-box solid, only the outer limits are constants; inner limits may depend on the outer variables.
chapters.leave: Coordinate changes go to 5.3; area and volume applications go to 5.5.

chapters.idea: Area is the double integral of 1, and volume is a triple integral of 1 or a double integral of height.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Area = ∬_D 1 dA, also in polar. Volume = ∭_E 1 dV, and volume under z = f(x,y) is ∬_D f(x,y) dA. Use polar for circular regions.

figure.aria: A flow from the disk r ≤ 1 to height 4−r², the polar integral, and volume 7π/2.

chapters.example: Find the volume under z = 4 − x² − y² over the disk x²+y² ≤ 1; the answer is 7π/2.
chapters.trap: Area uses integrand 1, not the height. In polar, the area element is r dr dθ, so the extra r changes the value.
chapters.leave: Surface area and mass applications go to Unit 6 or later topics.
